items.first: It's possible that Marco forgot about the meeting.
items.hint: Speculating about the past: modal + have + past participle.
items.explanation: 'May have + past participle' expresses a possibility about the past: perhaps Marco forgot. The past participle of 'forget' is 'forgotten'.

items.first: Although she had prepared thoroughly, she did badly in the interview.
items.after: thoroughly, she did badly in the interview.
items.hint: 'In spite of' is followed by a noun or an -ing form, never by a full clause.
items.explanation: 'In spite of' needs a noun or gerund: 'in spite of having prepared / preparing'. 'In spite she had prepared' is wrong.

items.first: People think that the government is considering a new tax on sugary drinks.
items.after: a new tax on sugary drinks.
items.hint: Passive reporting with a continuous action: is thought + to be + -ing.
items.explanation: When the reported action is in progress now, we use 'is thought + to be + -ing': the government is thought to be considering a new tax.

items.first: I'd prefer you not to mention this to anyone.
items.hint: 'Would rather + another person' is followed by a past tense.
items.explanation: When we want someone else to do (or not do) something, 'would rather' takes a past form with present meaning: I'd rather you didn't mention this.

items.first: We couldn't have finished the project on time without Laura's help.
items.after: , we couldn't have finished the project on time.
items.hint: Third conditional: If + past perfect, … could have + past participle.
items.explanation: This is a third conditional about an imaginary past: 'If Laura hadn't helped (us), we couldn't have finished'. The negative is needed because the help actually happened.

items.first: Nobody expected the team to win the league.
items.before: The team's victory in the league
answers: came as a complete surprise to
items.hint: Use the expression 'come as a surprise to someone'.
items.explanation: 'Something comes as a surprise to someone' means they did not expect it. Note the preposition 'to' before the person.

items.first: I've never seen such a beautiful sunset.
items.hint: Say it with a comparative: 'never seen a … sunset'.
items.explanation: 'I've never seen such a beautiful sunset' = 'I have never seen a more beautiful sunset': a comparative after 'never' means this is the best one.

items.first: The queue was so long that we gave up and went for lunch.
items.after: that we gave up and went for lunch.
items.hint: 'So + adjective' becomes 'such + a + adjective + noun'.
items.explanation: 'So' goes with an adjective alone (so long); 'such' goes with a noun phrase: 'It was such a long queue that…'.

items.first: Nobody told me that the hostel had no hot water.
items.after: that the hostel had no hot water.
items.hint: Make the sentence passive, with 'I' as the subject.
items.explanation: The passive of 'Nobody told me' is 'I wasn't told / I wasn't informed'. 'Inform' is more formal than 'tell' and fits the same structure.

items.first: Living with a host family helped me improve my Spanish enormously.
items.hint: Use the collocation 'make a difference to something'.
items.explanation: We 'make a difference to' something. 'Enormously' becomes an adjective before the noun: made an enormous / a huge difference.

items.first: I'll lend you my rucksack, but you must give it back by Friday.
answers: on the condition that you give
items.hint: Use the phrase 'on condition (that)' followed by a present tense.
items.explanation: 'On (the) condition that' means 'only if'. Like other conditional linkers, it takes a present tense for the future: on condition that you give it back.

items.first: As soon as we arrived in Prague, it started to snow.
items.after: Prague when it started to snow.
items.hint: 'Scarcely' goes between 'had' and the past participle, and is followed by 'when'.
items.explanation: 'Had scarcely + past participle… when…' means 'as soon as': we had scarcely arrived in Prague when it started to snow. With inversion it would be 'Scarcely had we arrived…'.

items.first: The coach didn't let the players use their phones before the match.
items.hint: 'Let' has no normal passive: use 'be allowed to'.
items.explanation: We can't say 'were not let use'. The passive of 'let somebody do' is 'be allowed to do': the players weren't allowed to use their phones.

items.first: It was wrong of the referee to send him off.
items.hint: Criticising a past action: should(n't) + have + past participle.
items.explanation: 'Shouldn't have + past participle' criticises something that happened: the referee sent him off, and that was a mistake.

items.first: Although he scored twice, the striker could not save his team from defeat.
items.before: The striker could not save his team from defeat
items.hint: 'Despite' is followed by a noun or an -ing form. The scoring happened before the defeat.
items.explanation: 'Despite' cannot be followed by a clause, so we use a gerund. The perfect gerund 'having scored' shows the goals came first. 'Despite scoring' is correct English but only two words.

items.first: I'm sure the manager was furious about the result.
items.hint: Being almost certain about the past: must + have + past participle.
items.explanation: 'Must have been' expresses a confident deduction about the past, the same meaning as 'I'm sure he was'.

items.first: People expect the new stadium to be finished next year.
items.hint: Passive reporting verb + to-infinitive, keeping the passive 'be finished'.
items.explanation: 'People expect X to be finished' becomes 'X is expected to be finished'. The second 'be' is needed because the stadium does not finish itself.

items.first: You will improve, but only if you train every day.
items.hint: A three-word expression that means 'only if'.
items.explanation: 'As long as' (or 'so long as') means 'on condition that'. Like 'if', it is followed by a present tense when we talk about the future.

items.first: I regret spending so much money on clothes last month.
items.after: so much money on clothes last month.
items.hint: 'If only' + past perfect expresses regret about the past.
items.explanation: 'If only I hadn't spent…' is a strong way of expressing regret about something in the past, like 'I wish I hadn't spent…'.

items.first: The bank refused to give me a loan.
items.hint: Which phrasal verb with 'turn' means 'refuse'? Make it passive.
items.explanation: 'Turn down' means 'refuse or reject'. The application did not refuse anything, so we need the passive: was turned down by the bank.

items.first: Prices have risen so much that many students can't afford to rent a flat.
items.after: that many students can't afford to rent a flat.
items.hint: Use the expression 'to such an extent / degree that…'.
items.explanation: 'To such an extent that' (or 'to such a degree that') is a formal way of saying 'so much that'.

items.first: It wasn't until I started working that I understood the value of money.
items.after: working did I understand the value of money.
items.hint: 'Not until + clause' at the start of a sentence is followed by inversion in the main clause.
items.explanation: 'Not until I started working did I understand…' puts the emphasis on the time. Note that the inversion ('did I understand') is already given after the gap.

items.first: My parents made me open a savings account when I turned eighteen.
items.after: open a savings account when I turned eighteen.
items.hint: In the active, 'make somebody do' has no 'to'. What happens in the passive?
items.explanation: 'Make somebody do something' becomes 'be made TO do something' in the passive: I was made to open a savings account.

items.first: There's no way I'm lending him money again.
items.hint: 'Under no circumstances' at the start of a sentence needs inversion.
items.explanation: Negative expressions such as 'Under no circumstances' at the beginning of a sentence are followed by inverted word order: will I lend.
